prerequisites.name: Electric charge and current
prerequisites.note: Current is the rate at which charge flows, measured in amperes.

prerequisites.name: Potential difference
prerequisites.note: A battery provides an energy difference per unit charge, measured in volts.

levelIntros.foundation: Think of voltage as the push that moves charge and resistance as how strongly the material opposes that push. Ohm's law links the three quantities in one equation.
levelIntros.intermediate: Ohm's law is a relationship between potential difference, current and resistance for a conductor at constant temperature. It connects a circuit measurement to the motion of charges inside the wire.
levelIntros.advanced: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, the ratio V/I is constant and defines resistance. This linear behaviour comes from a steady drift velocity reached when the electric force is balanced by collisions in the lattice.

alternate.heading: A water-pipe picture
alternate.body: Imagine charge as water flowing through pipes. The battery is the pump that creates a pressure difference, a thin section is high resistance, and the flow rate is the current. This picture is useful for series and parallel intuition, but it stops being literal at the atomic level: charge is not used up, and the wire already contains the charges that move.

sections.heading: The relationship
sections.body: Potential difference V across a conductor is directly proportional to the current I through it, provided the temperature stays constant. The constant of proportionality is the resistance R, so V = I R. Rearranged, I = V / R and R = V / I.

sections.heading: What resistance depends on
sections.body: Resistance is not just a property of the material. A longer wire has more resistance, a thicker wire has less, and a hotter metal usually has more. For a uniform wire, R = ρL/A, where ρ is the resistivity of the material, L its length and A its cross-sectional area.

sections.heading: Why the current is the same everywhere
sections.body: In a series circuit there is only one path, so charge cannot pile up or disappear. The same charge passes every cross-section each second. Components share the voltage instead: the total potential difference equals the sum of the potential differences across each component.

derivation.heading: Where the linear graph comes from
derivation.body: In a metal, electrons accelerate under the electric field but collide with ions. They quickly reach a steady drift velocity v_d proportional to the field E, so I ∝ E. Since E = V/L for a uniform wire, I ∝ V and the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin. The gradient is 1/R.

workedExample.problem: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. Find the current, then find the current if the resistance is doubled.
steps: Write the relationship: I = V / R.
Substitute the first values: I = 12 / 4 = 3 A.
Double the resistance: R = 8 Ω, with V still 12 V.
Substitute again: I = 12 / 8 = 1.5 A.
Check: doubling R at constant V halves I, which matches the equation.
workedExample.answer: 3 A, then 1.5 A. The current halves when the resistance doubles at constant voltage.

misconceptions.label: Current is used up by components
misconceptions.explanation: Charge is conserved. A component converts electrical energy into other forms, which lowers the potential difference, but the same current leaves the component as enters it in a series circuit.
misconceptions.remediation: Track charge, not energy: count what passes a point per second before and after the bulb.

misconceptions.label: A battery always supplies the same current
misconceptions.explanation: A battery maintains roughly a fixed potential difference, not a fixed current. The current is set by the resistance of the whole circuit.
misconceptions.remediation: Use I = V/R and change R while keeping V fixed to see the current change.

questions.prompt: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 Ω resistor. What current flows?
questions.expected: 3 A
questions.hint: Rearrange V = I R for the current.

questions.prompt: The resistance in a circuit is doubled while the battery voltage stays the same. What happens to the current, and why?
questions.expected: The current halves, because I = V/R and R doubled at constant V.
questions.explanation: Since I = V/R, doubling R at constant V makes I half as large. Current is inversely proportional to resistance.
questions.hint: Use I = V/R and substitute a doubled value.

questions.prompt: Two identical bulbs are connected in series with one battery. Why is each bulb dimmer than a single bulb on its own?
questions.expected: The total resistance is larger, so the current is smaller, and each bulb gets less power.
questions.explanation: Adding a second bulb in series increases the total resistance, so the battery drives a smaller current. With less current through each bulb, the power converted in each one falls, so each glows dimmer.
questions.hint: What happens to total resistance when you add a component in series?

questions.prompt: A wire is stretched so that its length doubles while its volume stays the same. What happens to its resistance? Show the reasoning.
questions.expected: It becomes four times larger: length doubles and area halves, so R = ρL/A increases by 2 / 0.5 = 4.
questions.explanation: Constant volume means L A stays fixed. Doubling L forces A to halve. R = ρL/A then changes by a factor 2 / (1/2) = 4. So the resistance becomes four times its original value.
questions.hint: If the volume is constant, what must happen to the cross-sectional area when the length doubles?

prerequisites.name: Vectors
prerequisites.note: Forces add as vectors, so direction matters as much as size.

prerequisites.name: Kinematics
prerequisites.note: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.

levelIntros.foundation: A net force changes how an object moves. The bigger the net force, the faster the change; the heavier the object, the slower the change.
levelIntros.intermediate: Newton's second law says the acceleration of an object is proportional to the net force on it and inversely proportional to its mass. It is a vector equation: the acceleration points in the direction of the net force.
levelIntros.advanced: The law is more generally stated as net force equals the rate of change of momentum, F_net = dp/dt. For constant mass this reduces to F_net = m a, and it holds only in an inertial frame.

alternate.heading: One net push on a trolley
alternate.body: Put the trolley on a smooth floor and push it. The push minus friction is the single net push that changes its speed. If you double the net push, the speed changes twice as fast; if you load the trolley with the same net push, it changes speed half as fast. This is why the equation is written for the net force, not for one individual force.

sections.heading: Net force, not just any force
sections.body: Add all forces on the object as vectors. If they cancel, the net force is zero and the velocity does not change. If they do not cancel, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force.

sections.heading: The equation
sections.body: F_net = m a, so a = F_net / m. Acceleration is measured in m/s². Doubling the net force doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass halves it for the same net force.

sections.heading: What the law does not say
sections.body: It does not say that a force is needed to keep moving. An object with zero net force keeps a constant velocity, which may be zero or non-zero. Friction and air resistance are forces too, so they must be included in the net force.

derivation.heading: From momentum to F = ma
derivation.body: Momentum is p = m v. Newton's second law in its general form is F_net = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt. When mass is constant this becomes m dv/dt = m a. For a variable-mass system, such as a rocket, the full momentum form must be used instead.

workedExample.problem: A 2 kg block is pushed with 10 N while friction opposes it with 2 N. Find the acceleration.
steps: Take the direction of motion as positive.
Net force = 10 N − 2 N = 8 N.
Use a = F_net / m.
Substitute: a = 8 / 2 = 4 m/s².
The acceleration points in the direction of the push.
workedExample.answer: 4 m/s² in the direction of the applied force.

misconceptions.label: Constant motion requires a constant force
misconceptions.explanation: A net force changes velocity; it is not required to maintain velocity. With zero net force, velocity stays constant. In everyday life friction makes it look as if a push is always needed.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the free-body diagram and check whether the forces actually cancel.

misconceptions.label: Mass and weight are the same
misconceptions.explanation: Mass measures inertia in kilograms and does not change with location. Weight is the gravitational force W = m g and is measured in newtons.
misconceptions.remediation: Label mass in kg and weight in N in every free-body diagram.

questions.prompt: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg object. What is its acceleration?
questions.expected: 5 m/s²
questions.explanation: a = F_net / m = 20 / 4 = 5 m/s².
questions.hint: Use a = F_net / m.

questions.prompt: A 5 kg box is pushed with 30 N and friction is 10 N. Find the acceleration.
questions.expected: 4 m/s², using the net force 20 N.
questions.explanation: The net force is 30 − 10 = 20 N, so a = 20 / 5 = 4 m/s². Using 30 N directly would ignore friction.
questions.hint: First find the net force, then divide by mass.

questions.prompt: The same net force acts on two objects, one twice as heavy as the other. Compare their accelerations and explain.
questions.expected: The heavier object accelerates half as much, because a = F/m.
questions.explanation: For the same net force, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. The heavier object has twice the mass, so it has half the acceleration.
questions.hint: Keep F fixed in a = F/m and double m.

questions.prompt: A car moves at a constant 60 km/h on a straight road. What is the net force on it, and why do the engine and friction both act?
questions.expected: The net force is zero because the velocity is constant; the engine force balances friction and air resistance.
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so F_net = m a = 0. The engine still does work against friction and air resistance, but those forces balance, so the net force is zero.
questions.hint: What does constant velocity tell you about acceleration, and therefore about net force?

packs.title: Reflection and image formation in a concave mirror

prerequisites.name: Law of reflection
prerequisites.note: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection, measured from the normal.

prerequisites.name: Similar triangles
prerequisites.note: Used to relate object distance, image distance and magnification.

levelIntros.foundation: A mirror changes the direction of light. A curved mirror can make light converge or spread out, which lets it form an image you can locate with a diagram.
levelIntros.intermediate: For a spherical mirror, parallel rays close to the principal axis converge at the focal point, with f = R/2. Ray diagrams use two standard rays to locate the image.
levelIntros.advanced: The mirror formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v and magnification m = −v/u follow from the paraxial approximation. Signs encode whether distances are measured in front of or behind the mirror, and the same rules reproduce whether an image is real or virtual.

alternate.heading: Trace one ray at a time
alternate.body: Instead of trying to remember the whole diagram, follow one ray and ask one question at each surface: where does it go after reflection? A ray parallel to the axis must pass through F; a ray through C must retrace itself. The image is simply where two reflected rays meet. If they only appear to meet behind the mirror, the image is virtual.

sections.heading: The three useful rays
sections.body: A ray parallel to the principal axis reflects through the focal point. A ray through the focal point reflects parallel to the axis. A ray through the centre of curvature reflects back along itself. Any two of these locate the image.

sections.heading: The mirror formula
sections.body: For a mirror, 1/f = 1/u + 1/v relates the focal length f, the object distance u and the image distance v. Real distances in front of the mirror are taken as positive in the school convention used here; a negative v means a virtual image behind the mirror.

sections.heading: Reading the result
sections.body: Magnification m = −v/u. A negative m means the image is inverted, and |m| tells you how many times larger or smaller it is. A virtual image is formed where reflected rays only appear to meet, so it cannot be caught on a screen.

derivation.heading: Why f = R/2
derivation.body: A ray parallel to the axis hits the mirror at height h. The normal at that point passes through the centre of curvature C. Using the small-angle (paraxial) approximation, the reflected ray crosses the axis at a distance f from the pole, and the geometry gives f = R/2. This fails for rays far from the axis, which is why real mirrors show spherical aberration.

workedExample.problem: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror with focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
steps: Use 1/f = 1/u + 1/v with u = 30 cm and f = 10 cm.
So v = 15 cm. It is positive, so the image is real and in front of the mirror.
Magnification m = −v/u = −15/30 = −0.5.
The image is real, inverted and half the object's height.
workedExample.answer: v = 15 cm, m = −0.5: a real, inverted, diminished image.

misconceptions.label: A virtual image cannot be seen
misconceptions.explanation: A virtual image can be seen by an observer because the reflected rays enter the eye as if they came from behind the mirror. It simply cannot be projected onto a screen.
misconceptions.remediation: Distinguish 'can be seen' from 'can be caught on a screen'.

misconceptions.label: Light rays actually pass through a virtual image
misconceptions.explanation: For a virtual image the reflected rays diverge. Their backward extensions meet behind the mirror; no light actually travels there.
misconceptions.remediation: Draw the reflected rays with arrows and use dashed lines only for the backward extensions.

questions.prompt: A concave mirror has focal length 10 cm. What is its radius of curvature?
questions.expected: 20 cm, because R = 2f.
questions.explanation: For a spherical mirror, the focal length is half the radius of curvature: f = R/2, so R = 2f = 20 cm.
questions.hint: How is f related to R for a spherical mirror?

questions.prompt: An object is 20 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image?
questions.expected: 20 cm in front of the mirror; the object is at the centre of curvature, so the image is real, inverted and the same size.
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20, so v = 20 cm. With the object at C, the image forms at C, inverted and the same size.
questions.hint: Substitute into 1/f = 1/u + 1/v.

questions.prompt: An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. Describe the image.
questions.expected: Virtual, erect and enlarged, behind the mirror.
questions.explanation: Rays from an object inside the focal length diverge after reflection. Their backward extensions meet behind the mirror, giving a virtual, erect, enlarged image. This is how a shaving mirror works.
questions.hint: Trace a ray parallel to the axis and a ray through the centre of curvature.

questions.prompt: An object 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm has height 4 cm. Find the image height and state its orientation.
questions.expected: Image height 2 cm, inverted (m = −0.5).
questions.explanation: From the previous calculation v = 15 cm, so m = −v/u = −0.5. The image height is |m| × 4 = 2 cm, and the negative sign means it is inverted.
questions.hint: Find m first, then multiply the object height by its magnitude.

prerequisites.name: Valence electrons
prerequisites.note: Only the outer-shell electrons are involved in bonding.

prerequisites.name: Electron pairs repel
prerequisites.note: Electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves as far apart as possible.

levelIntros.foundation: Atoms can share electrons to fill their outer shells. A shared pair is a covalent bond, and the number of shared pairs decides how many bonds an atom forms.
levelIntros.intermediate: A covalent bond forms when two atoms share a pair of electrons. The shape of the molecule is set by the arrangement of electron pairs around the central atom, not by the bonds alone.
levelIntros.advanced: Lewis structures account for sigma bonding and lone pairs, while VSEPR predicts geometry from electron-domain repulsion. Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference, and molecular polarity also depends on the vector sum of bond dipoles, which is why CO2 is non-polar but H2O is polar.

alternate.heading: Electron-pair balloons
alternate.body: Tie several balloons to one knot. They push each other away and settle into the most spread-out arrangement. Electron pairs around a central atom behave similarly: four pairs spread tetrahedrally, while a lone pair takes more room and squeezes the bonds together. Rotate the model and look for the balloon-like arrangement, then count atoms only to name the molecular shape.

sections.heading: Sharing, not transferring
sections.body: In a covalent bond the nuclei attract the same shared electron pair. Each atom counts the shared pair towards its outer shell. Covalent bonding typically occurs between non-metals, where neither atom gives up an electron completely.

sections.heading: Shape comes from electron pairs
sections.body: Electron pairs around a central atom repel and spread out. Two domains give a linear shape, three give trigonal planar, and four give tetrahedral. Lone pairs occupy space too and push the bonding pairs closer together.

sections.heading: Why shape matters
sections.body: Shape controls boiling point, solubility and how a molecule interacts with a receptor or another molecule. Two molecules with the same formula can have different shapes and very different properties.

derivation.heading: Predicting a shape with VSEPR
derivation.body: Count electron domains on the central atom: each bond (single, double or triple counts once) plus each lone pair. Arrange the domains to minimise repulsion. Then name the shape from the positions of atoms only. For water, oxygen has two bonds and two lone pairs: four domains, tetrahedral electron geometry, bent molecular shape, about 104.5°.

workedExample.problem: Predict the shape and bond angle of methane (CH4) and ammonia (NH3).
steps: Carbon in CH4 has four single bonds and no lone pairs: four domains.
Four domains arrange tetrahedrally, so CH4 is tetrahedral with 109.5° bond angles.
Nitrogen in NH3 has three single bonds and one lone pair: also four domains.
The lone pair repels more strongly than a bond pair, so the H–N–H angle is squeezed to about 107°.
The molecular shape counts atoms only, so NH3 is trigonal pyramidal.
workedExample.answer: CH4: tetrahedral, 109.5°. NH3: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.

misconceptions.label: Covalent bonds transfer electrons
misconceptions.explanation: Transfer of electrons produces ions and ionic bonding. A covalent bond shares an electron pair, and the pair is attracted by both nuclei.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare NaCl (transfer) with CH4 (sharing) using electron-dot diagrams.

misconceptions.label: Molecular shape does not matter
misconceptions.explanation: Shape determines polarity, intermolecular forces and biological activity. Bent water is polar and has a high boiling point; linear CO2 is non-polar despite polar bonds.
misconceptions.remediation: Add bond dipoles as vectors on the 3D model and see whether they cancel.

questions.prompt: How many covalent bonds does a carbon atom form in methane?
questions.expected: Four single covalent bonds.
questions.explanation: Carbon has four valence electrons and needs four more to complete its octet, so it forms four single covalent bonds in CH4.
questions.hint: Count the valence electrons carbon needs to reach eight.

questions.prompt: Why is the H–O–H bond angle in water about 104.5° rather than 109.5°?
questions.expected: Oxygen has two lone pairs, which repel the bonding pairs more strongly and squeeze the angle.
questions.explanation: Water has four electron domains, but two are lone pairs. Lone pairs occupy more space and repel bonding pairs more strongly, so the H–O–H angle closes to about 104.5°.
questions.hint: How many lone pairs does oxygen have in water?

questions.prompt: CO2 has polar C=O bonds but the molecule is non-polar. Explain why.
questions.expected: CO2 is linear, so the two equal bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.
questions.explanation: The C=O bonds are polar, but the molecule is linear with the two dipoles equal and opposite. Their vector sum is zero, so the molecule as a whole is non-polar.
questions.hint: Draw the bond dipoles as arrows and add them vectorially.

questions.prompt: Using VSEPR, predict the electron-domain geometry and molecular shape of NH4+.
questions.expected: Four bonding pairs and no lone pairs: tetrahedral electron geometry and tetrahedral molecular shape, angle 109.5°.
questions.explanation: The ammonium ion has four N–H bonds and no lone pair on nitrogen. Four domains give a tetrahedral arrangement, so both the electron geometry and the molecular shape are tetrahedral with 109.5° angles.
questions.hint: Remember the positive charge means nitrogen has gained a bond, not a lone pair.

prerequisites.name: Cell organelles
prerequisites.note: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and the membranes where the light reactions happen.

prerequisites.name: Energy in chemical bonds
prerequisites.note: Light energy is converted into chemical energy stored in glucose.

levelIntros.foundation: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Chlorophyll captures the light, and the glucose stores the energy.
levelIntros.intermediate: Photosynthesis has two linked stages: the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membranes and the light-independent Calvin cycle in the stroma. The first supplies ATP and NADPH to the second.
levelIntros.advanced: The light reactions split water at photosystem II, pump protons to build a gradient, and use chemiosmosis to make ATP while reducing NADP+. The Calvin cycle then fixes CO2 with RuBisCO, consuming ATP and NADPH. Overall, six CO2 molecules are fixed per glucose.

alternate.heading: A solar-powered factory
alternate.body: The leaf is a factory with two departments. The thylakoid department runs on sunlight, splits water and produces the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. The stroma department uses those carriers to build sugar from CO2. If the solar department stops at night, the sugar department soon runs out of power even though raw materials are still available.

sections.heading: The overall change
sections.body: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, with light absorbed by chlorophyll. The oxygen released comes from water, not from carbon dioxide. The glucose stores energy that the plant and the food chain use.

sections.heading: Two stages
sections.body: In the light reactions, water is split, oxygen is released, and ATP and NADPH are produced. In the Calvin cycle, CO2 is fixed using that ATP and NADPH to build sugars. The stages are linked: stopping the light reactions quickly stops the Calvin cycle.

sections.heading: Where and when
sections.body: Chloroplasts contain stacks of thylakoids surrounded by stroma. Light reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes; the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma. Photosynthesis needs light, but the Calvin cycle itself does not use light directly.

derivation.heading: Why oxygen comes from water
derivation.body: Isotope experiments using H2¹⁸O showed that the released oxygen is labelled, while CO2 labelled with ¹⁸O did not label the oxygen gas. This identified water as the electron donor at photosystem II: 2H2O → 4H+ + 4e⁻ + O2.

workedExample.problem: A plant fixes 12 molecules of CO2. How many glucose molecules can it build, and how much oxygen is released?
steps: The balanced equation needs 6 CO2 per glucose: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
12 CO2 is twice 6, so it can produce 2 glucose molecules.
Oxygen released is 6 per glucose, so 2 × 6 = 12 O2 molecules.
Check atom balance: 12 C, 24 H and 18 O on each side.

misconceptions.label: Plants photosynthesise only at night
misconceptions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires light, so it happens in daylight. Respiration happens all the time, day and night. At night only respiration occurs, which is why CO2 output can exceed uptake.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate the two processes: light drives photosynthesis, respiration is continuous.

misconceptions.label: The released oxygen comes from carbon dioxide
misconceptions.explanation: Isotope experiments show the O2 comes from splitting water. Carbon dioxide supplies carbon for glucose, not the oxygen gas.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the half-reaction at photosystem II and mark the source of each atom.

questions.prompt: Name the gas released during photosynthesis and the process that produces it.
questions.expected: Oxygen, released when water is split in the light reactions.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released when water is split at photosystem II during the light-dependent reactions.
questions.hint: Which molecule is split to provide electrons?

questions.prompt: Explain why a plant kept in darkness cannot continue making glucose for long, even though it has plenty of CO2 and water.
questions.expected: Without light, the light reactions stop producing ATP and NADPH, so the Calvin cycle cannot fix CO2.
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle needs ATP and NADPH from the light reactions. In darkness those supplies run out, so CO2 fixation stops even if CO2 and water are available.
questions.hint: What do the light reactions supply to the Calvin cycle?

questions.prompt: A plant is given water containing labelled oxygen (H2¹⁸O). Where does the label appear?
questions.expected: In the released oxygen gas, because water is split at photosystem II.
questions.explanation: Water is the electron donor at photosystem II, so its oxygen atoms become the O2 released. This is the isotope evidence that oxygen does not come from CO2.
questions.hint: Which molecule is split during the light reactions?

questions.prompt: A plant fixes 18 molecules of CO2. How many glucose and oxygen molecules result, and how did you balance it?
questions.expected: 3 glucose and 18 oxygen, using 6CO2 per glucose.
questions.explanation: The equation fixes 6 CO2 and releases 6 O2 per glucose. 18/6 = 3 glucose, so 3 × 6 = 18 O2. Balancing carbon first, then hydrogen and oxygen, confirms the counts.
questions.hint: Start from 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

steps: Light absorbed by chlorophyll
Water split, oxygen released
ATP and NADPH made
CO2 fixed in Calvin cycle
Glucose formed and stored

prerequisites.name: Factorisation
prerequisites.note: Splitting a quadratic into two linear factors gives its roots directly.

prerequisites.name: Coordinate geometry
prerequisites.note: The graph of a quadratic is a parabola in the coordinate plane.

levelIntros.foundation: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 with a not zero. Its solutions are the x-values where the graph crosses the x-axis.
levelIntros.intermediate: Every quadratic can be solved by factorising, completing the square or the quadratic formula. The discriminant b² − 4ac tells you how many real roots exist before you solve.
levelIntros.advanced: Completing the square rewrites ax² + bx + c as a(x + b/2a)² + (c − b²/4a). This exposes the vertex and yields the quadratic formula, while the discriminant determines whether the roots are real and distinct, equal, or complex conjugates.

alternate.heading: The bowl and the x-axis
alternate.body: Picture the parabola as a bowl standing on the x-axis. The bottom of the bowl is the vertex, and the two places where the rim crosses the axis are the roots. If the bowl is lifted above the axis, there are no real roots; if it just touches, there is one repeated root. Move the sliders and watch the bowl move rather than trying to memorise the discriminant.

sections.heading: Three ways to solve
sections.body: Factorise when the numbers cooperate, complete the square to reveal the vertex, or substitute into the quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. All three give the same roots when used correctly.

sections.heading: The discriminant
sections.body: D = b² − 4ac. If D > 0 there are two distinct real roots; if D = 0 there is one repeated real root; if D < 0 there are no real roots (the roots are complex). The parabola touches or misses the x-axis accordingly.

sections.heading: Reading the graph
sections.body: The vertex is at x = −b/(2a). Its y-value is the minimum when a > 0 and the maximum when a < 0. The axis of symmetry is the vertical line x = −b/(2a), so the roots are symmetric about it.

derivation.heading: Deriving the quadratic formula
derivation.body: Start with ax² + bx + c = 0 and divide by a. Complete the square by adding and subtracting (b/2a)². The equation becomes (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac)/4a². Take the square root of both sides and solve for x, giving x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a. This is also why the discriminant appears under the square root.

workedExample.problem: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 and describe its graph.
steps: Look for two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to −5: −2 and −3.
Factorise: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0.
So x = 2 or x = 3.
Check with the discriminant: D = 25 − 24 = 1 > 0, so two distinct real roots.
Vertex x = −b/2a = 5/2 = 2.5; y = 2.5² − 5(2.5) + 6 = −0.25. The parabola opens upward with minimum at (2.5, −0.25).
workedExample.answer: x = 2 and x = 3; an upward parabola with vertex (2.5, −0.25).

misconceptions.label: Every quadratic has two real roots
misconceptions.explanation: A quadratic always has two roots over the complex numbers, but it may have no real roots. When the discriminant is negative, the parabola does not cross the x-axis.
misconceptions.remediation: Compute the discriminant first and connect its sign to the graph.

misconceptions.label: The vertex is always a minimum
misconceptions.explanation: The vertex is a minimum only when a > 0. If a < 0 the parabola opens downward and the vertex is a maximum.
misconceptions.remediation: Use the sign of a to choose the opening direction before naming the vertex.

questions.prompt: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factorising.
questions.expected: x = 2 or x = 3
questions.hint: Find two numbers with product 6 and sum −5.

questions.prompt: For x² + 2x + 5 = 0, calculate the discriminant and state how many real roots there are.
questions.expected: D = 4 − 20 = −16, so there are no real roots.
questions.explanation: D = b² − 4ac = 4 − 4(1)(5) = −16. A negative discriminant means no real roots, and the parabola does not cross the x-axis.
questions.hint: Substitute a = 1, b = 2, c = 5 into b² − 4ac.

questions.prompt: A parabola has equation y = −2x² + 4x + 1. Is its vertex a maximum or a minimum? Find the x-coordinate of the vertex.
questions.expected: A maximum, at x = −b/2a = −4/(−4) = 1.
questions.explanation: Here a = −2 < 0, so the parabola opens downward and the vertex is a maximum. Its x-coordinate is −b/2a = −4/(−4) = 1.
questions.hint: The sign of a decides the opening direction.

questions.prompt: The roots of a quadratic are 2 and 5. Write an equation with these roots and explain how the coefficients relate to the roots.
questions.expected: x² − 7x + 10 = 0; the sum of roots is −b/a = 7 and the product is c/a = 10.
questions.explanation: (x − 2)(x − 5) = x² − 7x + 10. In general the sum of the roots is −b/a and the product is c/a, so 2 + 5 = 7 and 2 × 5 = 10.
questions.hint: Multiply (x − r1)(x − r2) and compare coefficients.

prerequisites.name: Coordinates
prerequisites.note: Points are located by an ordered pair (x, y).

prerequisites.name: Congruence and similarity
prerequisites.note: Congruent shapes are identical in size and shape; similar shapes have equal angles and proportional sides.

levelIntros.foundation: A transformation moves a shape on a grid. Translation slides it, rotation turns it, reflection flips it, and scaling changes its size.
levelIntros.intermediate: Each transformation can be described by a rule applied to every vertex. Translation adds a vector, rotation turns points about a centre, reflection flips across a line and enlargement multiplies distances from a centre.
levelIntros.advanced: Transformations can be represented by matrices acting on position vectors. Rotations and reflections are isometries, preserving distance and area. A scaling matrix changes area by the square of its scale factor, and the determinant of the matrix tells you that area multiplier.

alternate.heading: A paper cut-out on a grid
alternate.body: Cut a triangle from paper and place it on squared paper. Slide it without turning: that is translation. Stick a pin in one point and turn it: that is rotation. Flip it over a line: that is reflection. Trace the original and the image, then check which lengths and angles survived. Only the enlargement changes the side lengths.

sections.heading: Four standard moves
sections.body: Translation adds the same vector to every point. Rotation turns the shape through an angle about a fixed centre. Reflection flips it across a mirror line. Enlargement multiplies distances from a centre by a scale factor, making similar images.

sections.heading: What is preserved
sections.body: Translations, rotations and reflections are rigid motions: lengths, angles and area are unchanged, so the image is congruent to the original. Enlargement preserves angles but changes lengths and area, so the image is similar rather than congruent.

sections.heading: Describing a transformation fully
sections.body: Always state the type and the details: a translation needs its vector, a rotation needs its centre, direction and angle, a reflection needs its mirror line, and an enlargement needs its centre and scale factor.

derivation.heading: Area under scaling
derivation.body: A scale factor k multiplies both dimensions by k, so area is multiplied by k². This is why doubling the side of a square makes its area four times larger. The determinant of the 2 × 2 scaling matrix is k², which is exactly the area multiplier.

workedExample.problem: Translate triangle A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 3) by the vector (3, −2). Give the image coordinates and check the lengths.
steps: Add 3 to every x-coordinate and −2 to every y-coordinate.
AB = 3 units and A′B′ = 3 units; AC = 2 and A′C′ = 2, so the image is congruent.
workedExample.answer: A′(4, −1), B′(7, −1), C′(4, 1); the triangle is unchanged in size and shape.

misconceptions.label: Rotation and reflection are the same
misconceptions.explanation: A rotation preserves the orientation of the shape (the order of vertices around the shape). A reflection reverses orientation, so the image is a mirror version and cannot be reached by rotation alone.
misconceptions.remediation: Track the order of the vertices clockwise or anticlockwise before and after the move.

misconceptions.label: An enlarged shape is congruent
misconceptions.explanation: Enlargement changes lengths, so the image is similar, not congruent. Angles stay the same but area changes by the square of the scale factor.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a side length and the area before and after scaling.

questions.prompt: Point P(2, 5) is translated by the vector (−4, 3). What are the coordinates of P′?
questions.explanation: Add the vector to the coordinates: (2 − 4, 5 + 3) = (−2, 8).
questions.hint: Add the x-components and the y-components separately.

questions.prompt: Which transformations always produce a congruent shape, and which one can change the size?
questions.expected: Translation, rotation and reflection are congruent; enlargement changes size (similar, not congruent).
questions.explanation: Translations, rotations and reflections preserve all lengths and angles, so images are congruent. Enlargement multiplies lengths by the scale factor, producing a similar shape, not a congruent one.
questions.hint: Ask which transformations keep every length unchanged.

questions.prompt: A shape is enlarged by scale factor 3. What happens to its area? Explain.
questions.expected: The area becomes 9 times larger, because both dimensions are multiplied by 3.
questions.explanation: Each length is multiplied by 3, so area is multiplied by 3 × 3 = 9. Area scales with the square of the linear scale factor.
questions.hint: Area depends on two dimensions.

questions.prompt: A point is reflected across the line y = x. What is the image of (3, −1), and why does reflection reverse orientation?
questions.expected: (−1, 3). Reflection swaps the coordinates across y = x and flips the shape, reversing the order of the vertices.
questions.explanation: Reflecting across y = x swaps x and y, so (3, −1) becomes (−1, 3). A reflection reverses the clockwise order of the vertices, which is why it cannot be reproduced by a rotation.
questions.hint: On the line y = x, the x- and y-coordinates trade places.

prerequisites.name: Living things are made of cells
prerequisites.note: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

prerequisites.name: Diffusion and osmosis
prerequisites.note: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.

levelIntros.foundation: A cell is the smallest unit of life. Its parts, called organelles, each do a specific job, much like organs in a body.
levelIntros.intermediate: The cell membrane controls exchange, the nucleus stores genetic instructions, mitochondria release energy from food, and ribosomes build proteins. Plant cells add a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
levelIntros.advanced: Organelles are compartmentalised to keep incompatible reactions separate. The endomembrane system, including the nuclear envelope, ER and Golgi, handles protein and lipid traffic, while mitochondria and chloroplasts carry their own DNA, supporting the endosymbiotic theory.

alternate.heading: A cell as a small factory
alternate.body: The nucleus is the office holding the instructions, ribosomes are the assembly benches, mitochondria are the power station, and the membrane is the security gate. In a plant cell, chloroplasts are solar panels and the wall is the outer brick shell. Walk through the labelled diagram and assign each part a factory job; then explain why a muscle cell needs more power stations.

sections.heading: The shared parts
sections.body: All cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and genetic material. The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that controls exchange. The nucleus in eukaryotes holds DNA, and ribosomes assemble proteins.

sections.heading: Energy organelles
sections.body: Mitochondria release energy from glucose through respiration, producing ATP. Chloroplasts in plant cells capture light energy for photosynthesis. Both have double membranes, and both contain their own DNA.

sections.heading: Plant and animal cells
sections.body: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole. Animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts, and may have small, temporary vacuoles. Both have mitochondria, ribosomes and a nucleus.

derivation.heading: Why compartmentalisation matters
derivation.body: Different reactions need different conditions. Lysosomes keep digestive enzymes acidic and separate from the cytoplasm; the inner mitochondrial membrane hosts the electron transport chain. Compartmentalising these processes prevents interference and concentrates reactants, making the cell more efficient.

workedExample.problem: A muscle cell and a root hair cell are examined. Predict which organelles are especially abundant in each.
steps: Muscle contraction needs a continuous supply of ATP.
ATP is produced by mitochondria, so muscle cells contain many mitochondria.
Root hair cells absorb mineral ions by active transport, which also needs ATP.
They are underground and receive no light, so they have no chloroplasts despite being plant cells.
So: many mitochondria in both; chloroplasts absent in the root hair cell.
workedExample.answer: Both have many mitochondria; the root hair cell has no chloroplasts.

misconceptions.label: Plant cells do not have mitochondria
misconceptions.explanation: Plant cells respire day and night and therefore need mitochondria. They also have chloroplasts for photosynthesis; the two organelles work together.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a leaf cell and an animal cell organelle by organelle.

misconceptions.label: The cell wall and the cell membrane are the same
misconceptions.explanation: The cell wall is a rigid outer layer that gives support and shape. The cell membrane is the selectively permeable layer just inside it, which controls what enters and leaves.
misconceptions.remediation: Locate both layers on the labelled diagram and compare their functions.

questions.prompt: Which organelle releases energy from glucose in the cell?
questions.expected: The mitochondrion.
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration and release energy stored in glucose as ATP.
questions.hint: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?

questions.prompt: Give two structures present in a plant cell but absent in a typical animal cell, and state one function of each.
questions.expected: Cell wall (support and shape) and chloroplasts (photosynthesis); a large central vacuole is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall for support and shape, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and usually a large central vacuole. Animal cells do not have a cell wall or chloroplasts.
questions.hint: Think about support, photosynthesis and storage.

questions.prompt: Why does a muscle cell contain more mitochondria than a skin cell?
questions.expected: Muscle contraction needs much more ATP, so more mitochondria are needed for respiration.
questions.explanation: Muscle contraction repeatedly uses ATP, so the cell needs many mitochondria to release energy quickly. A skin cell has a much lower energy demand.
questions.hint: Link the organelle's function to the cell's job.

questions.prompt: A root hair cell has many mitochondria but no chloroplasts. Explain why both facts make sense.
questions.expected: It actively transports minerals, needing ATP from mitochondria; it is underground and receives no light, so chloroplasts would be useless.
questions.explanation: Root hair cells absorb mineral ions against a concentration gradient, which requires active transport and therefore ATP. They are below ground and receive no light, so chloroplasts would serve no purpose.
questions.hint: What process lets roots take up minerals, and does it need energy?
